# Escalation Protocol for Student Disclosures (template)

> **This is a template, not a policy.** Your school's counselor (or other pupil services
> professional) and your administration must adapt it to your school's crisis plan, safety
> plan, and board policies, and sign the approval block at the end, **before any Student uses
> the Library Assistant**. It is not legal advice. Fill every `[BLANK: …]`. Settle every
> `[VERIFY]` with the named person before you sign. Keep the filled-in copy in a
> district-controlled place, not in this public repository.

Words in **bold capitals** (Flag, Flag queue, Card number, and so on) mean exactly what the
Library Assistant's glossary says. They are explained where they first appear.

---

## The first ten minutes

**Print this page. Keep it next to the screen that shows the Flag queue.**

A **Flag** is the assistant's note that one exchange may involve self-harm, abuse, bullying, or
a threat of violence. It shows a category, a severity, the reason, the **Class label** (such as
"Period 3"), and the **Card number** (such as "card 14"). It does not show a name. The assistant
never knows who the Student is.

**1. Read the whole exchange in the Flag.** Not just the matched words. Decide: could someone be
hurt today?

**2. If anyone may be in danger right now** (a plan, a means, a time, "tonight", "I have a gun",
someone hurting them at home today, a threat to the school):

- If the Student may be hurting themselves or someone else **at this moment**, or a weapon is
  involved: **call 911**, then follow the school crisis plan: `[BLANK: crisis plan name and
  page]`.
- Otherwise get the Student's identity now (step 3), then **walk** to the
  Counselor or administrator. Do not send a message and wait.
  - Counselor: `[BLANK: name, room, phone/extension]`
  - Backup: `[BLANK: administrator name, phone/extension]`
- **Do not leave a Student at risk of suicide alone**, and do not let them leave school.
  Someone stays with them until the Counselor, a parent, or emergency services take over.

**3. Find out who it is (Identification).** Go to, or phone, the **Teacher** who holds the
**Roster** for that Class label. Ask: "Who had card `N` in `Class label` today?" Say it in
person or by phone, never in the assistant, never in email or chat.
Teacher for each Class label: `[BLANK: where the list of Class labels and Teachers is kept]`.

**4. Abuse or neglect?** If you now have reasonable cause to suspect a child has been abused or
neglected, **you** must report it **immediately, by phone or in person**, to county Child
Protective Services or law enforcement (Wis. Stat. 48.981). Telling the principal or the
Counselor does not satisfy your duty.
County CPS: `[BLANK: county CPS intake number]`. After hours: `[BLANK: after-hours number]`.

**5. Threat of violence at or toward the school?** If you believe in good faith there is a
serious and imminent threat, **you** must tell law enforcement **immediately, by phone or in
person** (Wis. Stat. 175.32). Police non-emergency: `[BLANK: number]`. Imminent danger: 911.

**6. Do not close the Flag yet.** An open Flag keeps the exchange past the end-of-day **Purge**.
Close it only when section 9 says you may.

**7. Write down what you did** in `[BLANK: the school's student-services record or incident
form]`, not in the assistant.

Crisis lines for anyone, any time: **call or text 988** (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline).
Emergency: **911**.

---

## 1. What this protocol is for, and what it is not

Middle school Students sometimes tell a chatbot what they will not tell an adult. The Library
Assistant is designed so that, when they do, an adult finds out and can help. It does this in
two ways:

- The **Watchlist**: a list of phrases and patterns, checked against every Student message, in
  real time, on every Install. A match raises a Flag immediately. For a high-severity match, the
  Student gets the **Supportive reply** (section 7) instead of an answer.
- **Oversight** (optional, only on some Installs): a second model that re-reads exchanges after
  they happen and raises Flags the Watchlist missed. Its Flags can arrive minutes or hours later
  (section 8).

**Flagging helps the adults do their duty of care. It does not replace it.** The Watchlist
will miss things: misspellings, slang it has not seen, a Student who hints instead of saying.
Everything you already do when a Student says something worrying (in the hallway, in an essay,
to a friend) still applies. This protocol only adds what is particular to the assistant: how a
concern reaches you without a name attached, and how you find the name.

This protocol sits under, and must agree with:

- the school safety plan required by Wis. Stat. 118.07(4): `[BLANK: title, date, where kept]`
- the suicide prevention and intervention procedure: `[BLANK: title, date, where kept]`
- the board's bullying policy required by Wis. Stat. 118.46: `[BLANK: policy number]`
- the board's child abuse and neglect reporting policy: `[BLANK: policy number]`
- the threat assessment procedure, if any: `[BLANK: title, team lead]`

Where they disagree, the school's plan wins and this template must be corrected.

school counselor or pupil services professional is part of every serious case.

## 3. Who watches the Flag queue, and how often

The **Flag queue** is the list of open Flags waiting for an adult. The assistant does not page
anyone, ring, or send email. A Flag sits in the queue until a person looks. So:

**Rule 1: No Student uses the assistant unless a named adult is watching the Flag queue.**
The assistant is for supervised use (one class at a time in the library, not whole-school
self-serve). Before each class session, the Librarian confirms who is watching. If the
Librarian has to step away, someone else signed in to the Flag queue takes over, or Students
stop using the assistant until the Librarian returns.

**Rule 2: Check the queue on this schedule.** Suggested defaults; the school sets its own.

| When | What | Who |
|---|---|---|
| While Students are using the assistant | Keep the Flag queue visible; look at least every `[BLANK: 10]` minutes, and at once when a Student looks upset or leaves suddenly | Librarian |
| At the end of each class session | Look through every Flag raised during that session before the class leaves, if you can; at the latest before the next class starts | Librarian |
| `[BLANK: 30]` minutes before the end-of-day Purge (`[BLANK: Purge time]`) | Last check of the day. Every high-severity Flag must have been acted on by now (section 4) | Librarian |
| First thing the next school day | Check for Flags raised overnight by Oversight (section 8) | Librarian |
| Librarian absent | Backup in section 2 does all of the above, or no Student sessions that day | `[BLANK]` |

**Rule 3: When a Flag needs the Counselor, Escalate it the same way every time.** If your
Install has a Counselor account, use Escalate in the Flag queue **and** tell the Counselor in
person or by phone. The Counselor sees only Escalated Flags, and only when they sign in, so the
button alone is not enough for anything urgent. If there is no Counselor account, walk or phone.

## 4. What to do, by how serious it is

The assistant marks each Flag with a severity from the Watchlist entry or from Oversight. That
severity is a starting point. **The adult reading the exchange decides how serious it is.** If
you are unsure, treat it as the more serious level.

### A. Imminent danger: right now

Signs: a plan, a method, access to means, a time ("tonight", "after school"), a goodbye, a
weapon, someone hurting the Student today, a specific threat to people at the school.

1. If anyone may be hurt in the next minutes, or a weapon is involved: **call 911** and follow
   `[BLANK: crisis plan section]`.
2. Identification at once (section 5). Locate the Student; they may still be in the room.
3. An adult goes to the Student and **stays with them**. Do not send them anywhere alone, not
   even to the counselor's office or the restroom. Bring them, or bring the Counselor to them.
4. Hand over to the Counselor or administrator in person. They follow the school's suicide
   intervention or threat procedure (risk assessment, parent or guardian contact, safety
   planning). If abuse by a parent or guardian is suspected, the Counselor follows CPS
   direction on whether and when the family is told.
5. Make any mandated report yourself (section 6). It is not a replacement for step 1.

### B. High severity: the same school day

Signs: talk of self-harm or suicide without the signs above; a disclosure of abuse or neglect;
serious or repeated bullying; a threat without specifics.

1. Within `[BLANK: 15]` minutes of seeing the Flag: Identification (section 5).
2. Before the Student leaves school today: the Counselor (or the Librarian wearing that hat)
   meets the Student, following the school's own procedure for that category.
3. Abuse or neglect: if you have reasonable cause to suspect it, report **immediately** to CPS
   or law enforcement (section 6). Do not wait for the Counselor's meeting.
4. Bullying: hand to `[BLANK: the employee the bullying policy names to investigate]` under
   policy `[BLANK]`. That policy decides parent notification.
5. If the Student has already gone home and you believe they may be at risk tonight: call the
   administrator on duty now. Do not leave it for tomorrow.

### C. Lower severity, or a Flag that is not a concern

Signs: a Watchlist match that was clearly something else (a book title, a history question about
war, a quote from a novel); mild unkindness; something worth a gentle check-in.

1. By the end of the school day, read the exchange and decide.
2. If it is not a concern: close the Flag and note why in one line (section 9). Do not do
   Identification just to be thorough. Not knowing who it was protects the Student's privacy.
3. If it is worth a check-in: tell the Counselor by the end of the day; they decide whether to
   do Identification.
4. If it was a Watchlist entry matching something harmless, tell the Watchlist owner (section 10)
   so the entry can be improved. Do not include the Student's words if they could identify them.

## 5. Identification: finding out who held the Card

The assistant cannot tell you who a Student is. It never had that information, by design. Each
Student uses a **Card**: a printed QR code with a **Card number** on it, handed out by a Teacher
for one class (a **Batch**, labelled with a **Class label** such as "Period 3"). Only the
**Teacher** who minted that Batch has the **Roster**: the list of which Student got which Card
number. The Roster lives on the Teacher's own computer.

**Identification** is one adult asking another:

1. Find the Teacher who registered that Class label. `[BLANK: how the Librarian knows which
   Teacher owns each Class label, for example a sign-up sheet at the library desk]`.
2. Ask in person or by phone: "Who had card `N` in `Class label` today?"
3. The Teacher looks it up in their Roster and tells you.
4. **Never type the name into the assistant.** Not in the Flag, not in a close note, not in a
   chat to test something. Never email or message "card 14 is [name]". The link between a
   Card number and a name exists only in the Teacher's Roster and in the adults' heads, and in
   the school's own record once the school opens one (section 9).
5. Tell only the people who need to act: the Counselor, the administrator, and anyone the
   law or the crisis plan requires. Federal student privacy law allows disclosure in a health or
   safety emergency to people who need it to protect the Student or others (34 CFR 99.36).

If the Teacher cannot be reached (absent, on a field trip): an administrator opens the sealed
Roster envelope for that Class label and date, kept in `[BLANK: where the office keeps sealed
Rosters]`, reads only the Card number needed, logs who opened it, when, and why, and reseals it
(ADR-0002, "a sealed printed Roster"). The office shreds each envelope when its Batch expires,
unless a Hold or an open Flag still needs it.

In imminent danger, the Student is often still in the room: a supervised class in the library,
with the Teacher present. Look first, ask the Teacher at once.

## 6. Mandated reporting under Wisconsin law

A Flag is **not** a report to anyone outside the school. The assistant reports nothing to CPS,
police, or parents. The duties below belong to people.

### Child abuse and neglect: Wis. Stat. 48.981

- **Who must report:** Wis. Stat. 48.981(2)(a) lists, among others, a school teacher, a school
  administrator, a school counselor, and "a school employee not otherwise specified in this
  paragraph". DPI's guidance says this means **all school employees**, including everyone who
  receives a W-2 from the school or district. The Librarian, the Teacher, and the Counselor are
  all mandated reporters.
- **When:** a person who "has reasonable cause to suspect that a child seen by the person in the
  course of professional duties has been abused or neglected", or has reason to believe the child
  has been threatened with abuse or neglect and that it will occur (48.981(2)(a)).
- **How and how fast:** the reporter "shall immediately inform, by telephone or personally, the
  county department" (CPS) or the sheriff or police department (48.981(3)(a)1). DPI's guidance:
  do not wait for a convenient time or the end of the day.
- **Telling school staff is not enough.** DPI: "Reporting to other school staff does not fulfill
  the duty to report." Do not assume someone else has reported. You may consult an
  administrator or pupil services professional first if they are immediately available, but if
  they are not, you must not wait, and the decision is yours.
- **Do not investigate.** Reasonable cause does not require proof. Once you have it, DPI advises
  asking no further questions. If you speak with the Student before you have it, use open
  questions ("What happened?" "What are you most worried about now?").
- **Protection and penalty:** a good-faith reporter is immune from civil and criminal liability,
  and good faith is presumed (48.981(4)). A reporter cannot be disciplined for a good-faith report
  (48.981(2)(e)). Intentionally failing to report can bring a fine of up to $1,000, up to 6 months
  in jail, or both (48.981(6)).
- **Training:** every school employee must have DPI's mandated reporter training within 6 months
  of starting and at least every 5 years (Wis. Stat. 118.07(5)).

**How a Flag relates to this duty.** A Flag is information that can give an adult reasonable
cause. When the adult who reads it (or learns of it through Identification) has reasonable cause
to suspect abuse or neglect, that adult must report, and must not wait for the Counselor to see
the Flag. The Teacher who does the Identification may also come to have reasonable cause, and
then also has the duty.

`[VERIFY]` with district legal counsel: whether a disclosure made through the assistant, before
Identification, is a child "seen by the person in the course of professional duties" under
48.981(2)(a). This template assumes the cautious reading: once the adults know who the Student
is, they treat it exactly like a disclosure made in person. Counsel should also confirm whether
to report straight away **without** a name when Identification is delayed. Never delay a report
of imminent danger to finish Identification: call 911 or CPS with what you know.

### Threats of school violence: Wis. Stat. 175.32

Everyone listed in 48.981(2)(a), so every school employee, "shall report" if they believe in good
faith, "based on a threat made by an individual seen in the course of professional duties
regarding violence in or targeted at a school, that there is a serious and imminent threat to the
health or safety of a student or school employee or the public" (175.32(2)(a)). The report goes
**immediately, by telephone or personally, to a law enforcement agency** (175.32(3)). Good-faith
reporters are immune; intentional failure to report carries the same penalty as above
(175.32(4), (5)). This is separate from, and in addition to, the school's threat assessment
procedure. The same `[VERIFY]` about "seen in the course of professional duties" applies.

### Suicide and self-harm

Wisconsin has no mandated-reporter statute for suicide risk the way it does for abuse. The
school's suicide intervention procedure governs. A school employee or volunteer who in good
faith tries to prevent a pupil's suicide is immune from civil liability for it (Wis. Stat.
118.295). If self-harm comes with signs of abuse or neglect at home, 48.981 applies as well.

### Bullying

The board's bullying policy (Wis. Stat. 118.46) names who investigates, requires employees to
report bullying, and requires that the parents or guardians of every pupil involved be
notified. Follow it. Bullying that includes a threat of violence also falls under 175.32;
bullying that includes abuse by a caregiver falls under 48.981.

## 7. The Supportive reply, and what the adult says next

When a Student's message matches a **high-severity** Watchlist entry, the assistant does not
answer the question. It sends the **Supportive reply** instead. Its text on this Install is:

> `[BLANK: paste the exact Supportive reply text shown on this Install. It tells the Student to
> talk to a counselor or a trusted adult, and gives the 988 line.]`

So, when you approach the Student, they have already been told to talk to a trusted adult. They
may expect you, or may be embarrassed that the computer "told". A low-severity match is silent:
the Student got a normal answer and does not know a Flag was raised. An Oversight Flag is also
silent (section 8).

What the adult says next is the Counselor's call, following the school's procedure. Some
starting points that agree with DPI and school-counselor guidance:

- Talk privately, calmly, and soon. "I wanted to check in with you. Can we talk somewhere quiet?"
- Be honest about how you know, without making the assistant sound like a trap. "Some of what
  you typed made me worried about you. I'd rather ask than guess."
- Ask directly about suicide when that is the concern. Asking does not put the idea in their
  head `[VERIFY]` with the Counselor against the school's training (QPR, DPI gatekeeper module).
  "Are you thinking about killing yourself?"
- Do not promise to keep it secret. "I can't keep this just between us if you might be unsafe,
  but I'll tell you who I'm telling and why."
- Tell the Student what happens next at each step, and stay with them if they are at risk.
- For a possible abuse disclosure, listen, thank them, and do not ask leading questions or push
  for details (section 6). "Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing."

Do not make the Student repeat what they typed as proof. Do not show them the transcript unless
the Counselor decides it helps.

## 8. Flags raised immediately versus hours later

The Flag queue shows which source raised each Flag and when.

| | Watchlist Flag | Oversight Flag |
|---|---|---|
| When it appears | The moment the Student sends the message | Minutes to hours after the exchange; on some Installs after class or after the school day |
| What the Student saw | High severity: the Supportive reply. Low severity: a normal answer | A normal answer. The Student has no idea anything was noticed |
| Where the Student is | Probably still in the library | May have left the library, the school, or gone home |
| Your first move | Look up: the Student is likely in the room | Check the time of the exchange and whether school is still in session |

**Oversight Flag, school still in session:** follow section 4 as usual. Identification is the
same. The Student may be in another class: the Counselor or administrator fetches them; do not
pull them out in front of the class with the reason.

**Oversight Flags arrive while the class is still here.** Oversight, when configured, screens
each message as the Student sends it, and the Student's next message waits for that screen
(ADR-0004). Cards last one school day at most and Sessions run only while someone is on Watch
(ADR-0010), so an Oversight Flag reaches the person on Watch within seconds, not overnight.
`[VERIFY]` with the Librarian whether Oversight on this Install is configured at all.

**If a Flag is raised after the Watch lapsed** (a dropped connection, not a schedule), it is
marked *raised unwatched* and its Alarm replays at the next Start watch. Treat it as section 4
says, starting with whether the Student is still in the building.

## 9. Record keeping

**The assistant holds only what the Flag holds:** the category, severity, reason, Class label,
Card number, the exchange, and when and by what it was raised. Nothing else about the case goes
into the assistant, ever: no names, no notes on the Student, no outcome of the Counselor's
meeting.

**What is written down, and where:**

| What | Where | Who |
|---|---|---|
| The Flag and its exchange | The assistant, until the Flag is closed and the next Purge runs | Automatic |
| Who the Student was | Nowhere new, unless the school opens a record (next rows) | |
| What the Librarian saw and did, with times | `[BLANK: the school's incident or student-services form]` | Librarian |
| Suicide risk assessment, parent contact, safety plan | `[BLANK: the counselor's records system]` | Counselor |
| A report to CPS or police | The reporter's own note of date, time, agency, and the name of the person taken the report, kept per `[BLANK: board policy]`. Reports are confidential under 48.981(7) | Reporter |
| Bullying investigation | Per the bullying policy | Named investigator |

**The Purge and its exception.** At the end of each school day (`[BLANK: time]`) the assistant
deletes every transcript, **except** those attached to an open Flag. Those stay until an adult
closes the Flag, and are deleted after that. So:

- **Before closing a Flag**, copy into the school's own record whatever the school needs from the
  exchange (for example, the Student's exact words, for a CPS report or the counselor's notes).
  After the Flag is closed and the Purge runs, the exchange is gone from the assistant for good.
- **Close a Flag when the adult action is finished:** Identification done or decided against,
  Counselor informed, reports made, record written. Note the reason in the Flag in one line
  without naming anyone: "Not a concern: book title", "Escalated to Counselor; handled per
  procedure".
- **Do not use open Flags as storage.** Aim to close every Flag within `[BLANK: 5]` school days.
  Any Flag open longer is reviewed by the Counselor.
- **If CPS, police, or counsel asks the school to keep the exchange,** tell the administrator and
  have the Librarian set a Hold on it before that day's Purge (ADR-0003, "Holds"), then Export
  it into the school's own records. Leaving the Flag open is not a way to keep it. `[VERIFY]` with
  district counsel when the Hold may be lifted.

A transcript tied to a named Student may be a pupil record under Wis. Stat. 118.125 and FERPA,
which is why the assistant is built never to hold that link. Once the school's own record names
the Student, that record follows the school's pupil-records rules like any other.

## 10. The Watchlist: owner, review, and misses

The **Watchlist** is the list of phrases and patterns the assistant checks every Student message
against, each tied to a category and a severity. It is the only source of an immediate Flag and
the only source of the Supportive reply. On most Installs it is the only source of Flags at all.
A miss is a Watchlist problem, and the school owns its copy.

**Owner:** `[BLANK: name and role]`, normally the Counselor working with the Librarian. The owner
approves every change and keeps a dated record of which Watchlist version is in use.

**Before first use:** a school counselor reviews the starter Watchlist for the euphemisms, slang,
and misspellings Students at this school actually use, and adds local ones.

**Reviewed at least:**

- once each semester: `[BLANK: dates, for example the first week of September and of
  February]`;
- after any **miss**, within `[BLANK: 10]` school days;
- when a new slang term, trend, or local incident comes up that Students might write about.

**What counts as a miss:** an adult learns, by any route, that a Student told the assistant
something in the Rubric (self-harm, abuse, bullying, threats of violence) and no Flag was raised,
or a Flag was raised far too low. Also count Flags that should have been high severity, and
entries that keep matching harmless things (false alarms wear people out).

**How a miss is reported:**

1. Whoever notices tells the Watchlist owner the same day, in person or by phone. Act on the
   Student's safety first (section 4); the Watchlist comes second.
2. The owner writes down, in `[BLANK: the Watchlist change log]`, the date, the category, and the
   **pattern** that was missed, in words that cannot identify anyone: "'unalive' plus a
   misspelling was not caught", not the Student's sentence.
3. The owner updates the Watchlist on this Install, or asks the Librarian to.
4. If the miss is likely to happen at other schools too, the Librarian may suggest the pattern to
   the Library Assistant project, **with no Student words, names, Card numbers, Class labels,
   dates, or school details**. The project's repository is public.

## 11. Before any Student uses the assistant

All of these must be true. The Librarian keeps this checklist signed and dated.

- [ ] Every `[BLANK]` in this document is filled in, and every `[VERIFY]` is settled.
- [ ] The Counselor and administration have approved this protocol (section 12).
- [ ] The Librarian, every Teacher who mints Cards, and the Counselor have read it.
- [ ] Each of them has current DPI mandated reporter training, including threats of school
      violence (Wis. Stat. 118.07(5)).
- [ ] The counselor has reviewed the Watchlist (section 10) and a version is recorded.
- [ ] The Librarian has tested a Watchlist match on the Install with no Students present, and
      seen the Flag and the Supportive reply.
- [ ] "The first ten minutes" page is printed and beside the Flag queue screen.
- [ ] Each Teacher knows to keep their Roster reachable during and after the class session, and
      what to do when asked for Identification.
- [ ] Parents and guardians have been told, in the school's notice about the assistant, that
      adults review what Students type and act on safety concerns. `[BLANK: where this notice
      is]`
- [ ] Students are told, in plain words before their first session, that adults can read what
      they type and will help if something worries them.

## Open questions this template depends on

These are product or policy questions that the school (and the Library Assistant project)
should settle. They are listed so nobody assumes the assistant handles them.

- The assistant does not alert anyone. A Flag waits until someone looks. Section 3 covers this
  with people and a schedule.
- When the Teacher is absent, Identification uses the sealed printed Roster in the office
  (section 5).
- The Supportive reply is one fixed text, built around suicide and self-harm (988). It may not fit
  an abuse disclosure or a threat of violence equally well. Check its wording (section 7).
- Closing a Flag lets the next Purge delete the exchange. The school must copy what it needs
  first (section 9).
